newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh has highest lead pollution in world.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh has highest lead pollution in world.

text.p: Bangladesh has the highest lead pollution in the world for part of the year, scientists at the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission (BAEC) said on Tuesday.
A 17-month study by BAEC scientists detected 463 nanogram (billionth of a gram) of lead, per metre of air over Dhaka during the dry months (November-January).

"Bangladesh has the highest lead pollution in world -- the figure appears to be the world's highest against 383 nanogram in Mexico city and 360 in Bombay," said BAEC's chief scientific officer, Dr. Mohammad Khaliquzzaman, who led the survey.
"It's alarming. Higher levels of lead are dangerous for child health", said Khaliquzzaman, who blamed the problem largely on the use of leaded fuel.
In Bangladesh, all vehicles use leaded fuel because the country's only refinery is not able to produce lead-free fuel, he said.
However, he said, the concentration of lead drops as the rainfall increases after the dry season.
"It comes down to 253 nanograms during the medium railfall period (February-May) and to 160 nanograms in the peak rainy months (June-August)," Khaliquzzaman told Reuters.
BAEC scientists said lead can penetrate into the lungs and subsequently into the blood. The heavy metal can also cause intellectual impairment in children,
"Lead can severely impair intelligence of children, can cause respiratory problems and annemia," said doctor Mizanur Rahman, a paediatrist in Dahaka's Post Graduate Medicine and Research Hospital.
Scientists and public health officials are also battling deadly water pollution in parts of Bangladesh.
Up to 15 people have died in recent months in the country's southern districts due to poisoning by the high content of arsenic in sub-soil water.
Authorities have hurriedly sealed many wells after water they pumped out tested "arsenic positive," doctors in the worst-affected districts said.
Dr. Fazlul Huq, a civil surgeon, said patients attacked by arsenic poisoning suffered "chronic skin rashes and deteriorating health."
"So far, no one seemed sure about what has led to the heavy arsenic concentration," he told reporters.
"The battle is on, but winning it is not that easy," said one official at the government's public health depeartment.
One scientist said diarrhoea caused by polluted water was perhaps the biggest child killer in Bangladesh.
